safety_warnings: Keep BOTH hands clear — two needles are active simultaneously
Never attempt to remove jammed fabric while powered on
Ensure BOTH needle guards are fitted before starting
Check thread tension on both needle paths before each shift
usage_steps: Thread both needle paths following the dual-path guide on the machine head
Lower the presser foot completely before starting
Run a test stitch on scrap fabric to verify both needle tensions are equal
Use the knee lever to lift the foot between seams

safety_warnings: STAND CLEAR of the clamping frame during automated cycles — it moves automatically
Never reach into the work area while the machine is running a programme
Ensure the fabric clamp is fully locked before pressing the start button
Only trained operators should modify stitch programmes
usage_steps: Load the correct programme for the pattern being sewn
Place fabric flat within the clamp area and lock the clamp
Confirm the thread is seated correctly in all tension guides
Press the start button and step back until the cycle completes

safety_warnings: Keep fingers away from the clamp foot — it descends automatically
Do not hold fabric tightly during the automated bartack cycle
Ensure the knife is lowered safely before cleaning thread debris
usage_steps: Position the reinforcement area (belt loop, pocket corner) under the clamp
Press the foot pedal to lower the clamp and start the cycle
Wait for the full automated stitch cycle to finish before repositioning
Remove finished piece after the clamp lifts

Blind stitch.typical_models: Juki SL718-2, Yamato CM-352, Brother JC-9330, Jack JK-T641-2A
safety_warnings: The curved needle is unique — standard needle guards do not cover it fully
Never run your finger under the fabric guide while the machine is powered on
Thread only using the correct curved-needle threading path
usage_steps: Fold the fabric hem to the required depth and use the fabric guide to hold it
Feed the folded hem under the curved needle slowly and evenly
Operate at medium speed — the curved needle is more fragile than straight needles
Check the blind stitch on the outer face after every seam

safety_warnings: Buttons can eject at high speed if misaligned in the clamp — wear eye protection
Never place fingers near the button holder while the foot pedal is engaged
Check that the button is fully seated in the clamp before starting
usage_steps: Set the stitch count and width to match the button hole pattern
Place the button in the button holder clamp securely
Position the fabric under the presser foot and lower it
Press the foot pedal to run the automated button-attachment cycle

safety_warnings: The built-in knife cuts the buttonhole automatically — never reach in during operation
The clamping foot moves automatically — keep fingers on the fabric edges only
Confirm buttonhole size is set correctly before running — mismatch can damage fabric
usage_steps: Set the buttonhole length using the size adjustment dial
Place the garment area flat under the clamp
Press the foot pedal — the machine will stitch and cut automatically
Check the finished buttonhole for clean edges before moving on

Cutter.typical_models: Eastman Straight Knife, KM RS-100, Gerber/Lectra CNC Cutter
safety_warnings: ALWAYS wear cut-resistant gloves when operating a straight or round knife cutter
Never cut toward your body — always cut away
Keep the blade guard in position when not actively cutting
For CNC cutters: stay clear of the cutting head movement zone during operation
usage_steps: Lay the fabric stack flat and smooth, ensuring no folds or wrinkles
Place the paper pattern or marker sheet on top
For straight knife: guide the machine slowly along pattern lines with steady pressure
For CNC cutter: load the marker file and confirm the vacuum table is active before starting

safety_warnings: The cylindrical arm is at table height — watch for leg/knee contact
Multiple thread paths increase tangle risk — check all cones before starting
Never pull tubular garments off the arm while the machine is running
usage_steps: Thread the machine following the multi-thread path diagram on the machine body
Slide the tubular garment section onto the cylindrical arm
Align the seam edges and lower the presser foot
Operate at medium speed and guide the garment off the arm end evenly
hazards: Chain-stitch unravelling if last stitch not secured

Flatlock Coverstitch.typical_models: Juki MF-7524, Yamato VG2700-8F, Pegasus FS713P-G0, Pegasus W562-01CB
safety_warnings: Multiple needles — keep ALL fingers away from the needle bar area
The cutting blade for the cylinder-bed variant is active — guard must be in place
Ensure the cover plate is closed before running — the looper mechanism moves at high speed
usage_steps: Thread all needle cones and looper following the colour-coded path guide
For cylinder-bed: slide the sleeve or cuff onto the arm before positioning under needles
Run a test stitch on scrap knit fabric to verify even tension across all needles
Guide fabric at consistent speed — uneven feeding causes skipped stitches on knitwear
hazards: Active cutting blade on cutter models

Multi-needle chain stitch.typical_models: Kansai Special DFB Series, Siruba VC008
safety_warnings: Never touch ANY of the needles while the machine is powered — they act together
The puller mechanism behind the needles is a pinch point — keep fabric edges only
Chain-stitch seams can unravel from the last stitch — always secure chain ends
usage_steps: Thread each needle individually, matching thread colour to the cone holder position
Feed the elastic or fabric edge under all needles at the same time
Engage the puller to assist even feeding at the correct rate
After finishing, pull sufficient chain off the back and knot or secure it before cutting

Overlock Serger.typical_models: Juki MO-6914S, Juki MO-6900S, Yamato CZ6020, Siruba SR747D, Pegasus E32-420
safety_warnings: The trimming knife is active at all times — NEVER slide fingers along the left fabric edge
Do not reach into the looper cover area while powered on
Multiple thread cones can unwind and tangle — check all cones are seated before starting
usage_steps: Thread the machine following the numbered path guide (loopers first, then needles)
Place the fabric edge against the right-hand guide plate
Lower the presser foot and begin feeding — the knife will trim automatically
Run a chain-off stitch on scrap after each seam to avoid thread pullback
hazards: Active trimming knife on left edge

Single-needle lockstitch.typical_models: Juki DDL-8700, Juki DDL-5550N-7, Brother DB2-B755, Singer ZOJE-ZJ8500G
safety_warnings: Always keep your fingers at least 5 cm from the needle while the machine is running
Ensure the needle guard/finger guard is fitted before each shift
Never attempt to remove fabric by pulling — always stop the machine first
usage_steps: Power on using the side switch and allow the servo motor to initialise
Load the bobbin and thread the upper path following the numbered guides
Lower the presser foot using the knee lever before starting to sew
Operate the speed foot pedal gently for precision seams

safety_warnings: The folder attachment moves automatically — do not hold fabric tightly through the folder
Multiple needles require ALL needle guards to be in place
Waistband feeding requires consistent tension — sudden jerks can break needles
usage_steps: Set the folder attachment to the correct waistband width
Feed the waistband fabric into the folder and align with the front guide
Attach the waistband start to the trouser/skirt and lower the presser foot
Guide at a consistent speed — the folder will curl and feed the waistband automatically

Zigzag stitching.typical_models: Juki LZ-2290A-SR-7, Juki LZ-2284A-7, Juki LZ-2287A
safety_warnings: The needle swings left and right — keep fingers further from the needle than on a standard lockstitch
Use only the correct wider throat plate designed for zigzag — a standard plate will cause needle breakage
Check stitch width setting before starting — wrong width causes needle strike on the foot
usage_steps: Set the stitch width and length using the dials on the machine body
Use the correct zigzag presser foot (wider opening than standard)
Test stitch on scrap fabric to confirm the needle clears both sides of the foot opening
Feed fabric at an even speed — zigzag stitching is more sensitive to speed variation
hazards: Needle strike risk if wrong foot used
